chapters.name: Chapter 1: Breeding for a better herd

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing breeds for your climate and market
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a breed or cross that fits your climate, your feed and your buyers.
This lesson builds toward: Given your climate, feed supply and market, you will choose a breed or cross for your farm and give reasons for the choice, naming at least three reasons that fit your farm.
The best breed is the one that makes money on your farm, not the one with the biggest numbers in a brochure. A high-yielding exotic dairy cow needs a lot of good feed, clean water, shade and close health care. In a hot, dry area with poor grazing, she may give less milk than a hardy local cross and fall sick more often.
Local breeds, such as the East African Zebu, the West African Dwarf goat or the N'Dama cattle of West Africa, cope with heat, ticks and poor feed but grow and yield less. Exotic breeds, such as Friesian or Ayrshire dairy cattle, Large White pigs or commercial hybrid chickens, yield more when you can feed and protect them well. Crosses often sit in between.
Start from your market: who buys, what they pay for (milk, live weight, lean meat, eggs, a festival goat) and when. Then check what you can supply all year: feed, water, housing, labour and a vet. Ask your extension officer, a breeders' association or your national research institute which breeds do well in your area. FAO's DAD-IS database lists the breeds kept in each country.
Step by step:
- Write what your buyers want and pay for.
- Write what you can provide all year: feed, water, housing, labour, vet.
- List two or three breeds or crosses that farmers near you keep.
- Ask your extension officer or a breeders' association about each one.
- Choose the breed that fits both lists, and write three reasons.
Words to know:
- Breed: a group of animals of one kind with the same looks and traits, passed from parents to young.
- Exotic breed: a breed developed in another region, often higher-yielding but less suited to local heat, disease and feed.
- Cross: an animal whose parents are from two different breeds.
Official sources:
- FAO DAD-IS: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (breed information by country)
Try it now: Write two short lists for your farm: what your buyers want, and what you can provide all year. Name two breeds or crosses and choose one, with three reasons.
You can now choose a breed or cross that fits your climate, your feed and your market, and explain why.

check.q: A farmer in a hot, dry area with poor grazing wants dairy cows. Which choice fits best?
options: The highest-yielding exotic cow he can find
Any cow that is cheapest at the market
A hardy local cross that suits the heat and the feed
A breed chosen from a brochure photo
check.why: A breed that copes with the heat and the feed he really has will produce more over time than one that needs inputs he cannot supply.

check.q: What should you write down FIRST when choosing a breed?
options: The name of the breed your neighbour likes
What your buyers want and pay for
The breed with the biggest animals
check.why: The market decides what pays; then you check what your farm can supply.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Heat detection and breeding records
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot a female in heat and record heats, services and due dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using a notebook or phone during twice-daily checks, you will record heat signs, services and expected due dates for each breeding female, with no missing dates for the animals you breed.
A cow, goat or sow can only conceive for a short time when she is "in heat". Miss it, and you wait about three weeks for the next one, while you still feed her. Cows, goats and pigs usually come into heat about every 21 days, but this varies, so watch closely.
The surest sign in a cow is standing heat: she stands still when another animal mounts her. Other signs are mounting other animals, restlessness, bellowing, a clear sticky discharge from the vulva and less milk. Goats wag their tails, bleat and seek the buck. A sow in heat stands still when you press on her back. Watch at least twice a day, early morning and evening, for 20 to 30 minutes, when animals are calm.
Records turn guesses into a plan. For each female write: her ID, the date and time of each heat, the date she was served, by which bull, buck or boar or which AI straw, and the expected due date. Then you know when to check for a return to heat about 3 weeks later, when to dry off a cow, and which females keep failing to conceive. Gestation is about 9 months for a cow, about 5 months for a goat, and about 3 months, 3 weeks and 3 days for a sow; your vet or extension officer can give the exact figures for your breed.
Step by step:
- Give every breeding female an ID: ear tag, name or number.
- Watch for heat twice a day, morning and evening.
- Write the date, time and signs you saw.
- Write the service date and the male or AI straw used.
- Add the date to check for a return to heat, about 3 weeks later.
- Write the expected due date, and check pregnancy with your vet or technician.
Words to know:
- Heat (oestrus): the short time when a female will accept the male and can become pregnant.
- Standing heat: when a cow stands still to be mounted; the surest sign she is in heat.
- Service: mating, by a male or by artificial insemination.
- Gestation: the time from conception to birth.
Official sources:
- University of Georgia Extension: Heat detection strategies for dairy cattle (standing heat, AM-PM rule)
Try it now: Make a breeding record page on paper or in a phone note with these columns: animal ID, heat date and time, signs seen, service date, male or AI straw, return-to-heat check, due date. Fill it in for one of your females, or an example cow.
You can now spot the signs of heat and keep a breeding record with heats, services and due dates.

check.q: Which is the surest sign that a cow is in heat?
options: She stands still when another animal mounts her
check.why: Standing to be mounted is the surest sign of heat; other signs only suggest it.

check.q: Your goat was served on 1 March. When do you watch for a return to heat?
check.why: Heats come about every 21 days, so a female that did not conceive shows heat again about 3 weeks later.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Artificial insemination and avoiding inbreeding
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Arrange AI with a trained technician at the right time, and plan matings that avoid close relatives.
This lesson builds toward: When a cow or goat shows standing heat, you will arrange artificial insemination with a trained, registered AI technician at the right time, calling the technician the same day and recording the semen or sire details. Given your breeding records, you will plan matings that avoid breeding close relatives, with no parent-offspring or brother-sister matings in the plan.
Artificial insemination (AI) places semen from a proven male into the female's reproductive tract. It gives a small farmer the genes of a top bull or buck without keeping one, and it lowers the risk of diseases spread by mating. AI is done by a trained AI technician or vet, not by the farmer. A wrong technique can injure the animal, and semen must be kept frozen in liquid nitrogen until the moment of use, or it dies.
Find a technician who is trained and registered: ask your county or district livestock office, your dairy cooperative or a registered vet. In Kenya, KAGRC supplies semen through appointed agents and AI technicians should be registered with the Kenya Veterinary Board; in Nigeria, check that the vet is on the Veterinary Council of Nigeria register. A common rule for cows is AM-PM: a cow first seen in standing heat in the morning is served that afternoon or evening; one first seen in the afternoon is served the next morning. Call the technician as soon as you see heat, and write down the straw's bull name or code.
Inbreeding means mating close relatives: a father with his daughter, a mother with her son, or a brother with his sister. The young are often weaker, grow slowly, get sick more and may be born with defects. It happens quietly when the same bull, buck, boar or cock stays on a farm for years. Prevent it: keep records of every animal's mother and father, swap or sell your breeding male before his daughters are old enough to breed, borrow or exchange males with farmers whose animals are not related to yours, and use AI straws from a different bull each time you breed a daughter.
Step by step:
- See standing heat: write the time.
- Call your registered AI technician at once.
- Use the AM-PM rule for cows, or the technician's advice.
- Check that the straw comes from a known bull and write its name or code.
- Before each mating, check the records: is this male her father, son or brother?
- If yes, use another male or a different AI bull.
Words to know:
- Artificial insemination (AI): putting semen from a chosen male into a female by hand, done by a trained technician.
- Straw: a thin tube holding one dose of frozen semen, labelled with the bull's name or code.
- Liquid nitrogen: a very cold liquid that keeps semen frozen until use.
- Inbreeding: mating close relatives, which makes weaker young with more defects.
Official sources:
- University of Georgia Extension: Heat detection strategies for dairy cattle (standing heat, AM-PM rule)
- Kenya Animal Genetic Resources Centre (KAGRC): semen and AI supplies
- Kenya Veterinary Board (register of vets and veterinary para-professionals)
- Veterinary Council of Nigeria (register of veterinary surgeons)
- ILRI: Training of AI service providers on community-based artificial insemination
Try it now: Write the name and phone number of a trained, registered AI technician near you (ask your livestock office or cooperative). Then look at your animals: list any female that is closely related to your current breeding male, and write how you will breed her instead.
You can now arrange AI with a trained technician at the right time and plan matings that avoid close relatives.

check.q: A cow shows standing heat at 7 am. Using the AM-PM rule, when should she be served?
options: Only when she stops showing heat
check.why: A cow first seen in heat in the morning is served that afternoon or evening.

check.q: Your bull has been on the farm for four years and his daughters are now ready to breed. What do you do?
options: Use him only on the biggest daughters
Use a different bull or AI from an unrelated bull for his daughters
check.why: Mating a bull with his daughters is inbreeding; an unrelated male or a different AI bull avoids it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Your biosecurity plan: zones, footbaths and visitors
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw your farm's biosecurity zones and write rules for footbaths and visitors.
This lesson builds toward: For your own farm or unit, you will write a biosecurity plan with zones, a footbath, visitor rules, quarantine and dead animal disposal, covering all five parts on one page.
Biosecurity means everything you do to stop germs getting onto your farm, spreading inside it, and leaving it. Most diseases arrive on animals, people, shoes, clothes, vehicles, crates, feed bags or equipment. Many of the best measures cost little: a fence, a gate, a footbath, soap and a rule that is kept every day.
Divide the farm into zones. The clean zone is where the animals live: only the people who care for them go in. The buffer zone is around it: the store, the changing area, the footbath. The dirty zone is outside: the road, the parking place, the market crates. Have ONE entry point to the animal area, with a gate you can close. Traders' trucks stay outside the fence; load and unload at the boundary.
At the entry, put a footbath with a farm disinfectant mixed as the label says, and change it when it is dirty or after rain; dirt stops disinfectant working, so brush the mud off boots first. Better still, keep farm-only boots and clothes at the entry. Have soap and water for hands. Keep visitors to those who must come, ask where they have been with animals, and write each visit in a visitor log: date, name, phone, reason and last farm visited.
Step by step:
- Sketch your farm: houses, pens, store, gate and road.
- Mark the clean, buffer and dirty zones.
- Choose one entry point to the animal area, with a gate.
- Put a footbath and handwashing point at that entry.
- Keep farm-only boots and clothes there if you can.
- Start a visitor log and keep traders' vehicles outside the fence.
Words to know:
- Biosecurity: steps that stop germs getting onto a farm, spreading on it and leaving it.
- Footbath: a shallow tray of disinfectant that people step through to clean their boots.
- Disinfectant: a chemical that kills germs; use a farm product mixed as the label says.
- Visitor log: a book where you write every visitor's name, contact, reason and last farm visited.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good practices for biosecurity in the pig sector (Animal Production and Health Paper 169)
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Sketch your farm on paper. Mark the clean, buffer and dirty zones, the one entry point, the footbath and where trucks will stop. Write three visitor rules under the sketch.
You can now draw biosecurity zones for your farm and set rules for footbaths, handwashing and visitors.

check.q: A pig trader arrives to buy weaners. Where should his truck stop?
options: Outside the fence, loading at the boundary
check.why: Vehicles that visit many farms carry germs, so they stay in the dirty zone outside the fence.

check.q: Your footbath is full of mud after the rain. What do you do?
options: Empty it, clean it and refill it with disinfectant mixed as the label says
Remove it until the dry season
check.why: Dirt and dilution stop a disinfectant working, so a dirty footbath must be cleaned and refilled.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Quarantine for new animals and safe disposal of the dead
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up quarantine for new animals and a safe way to dispose of dead ones.
This lesson builds toward: For your own farm or unit, you will write a biosecurity plan with zones, a footbath, visitor rules, quarantine and dead animal disposal, covering all five parts on one page.
New animals are the most common way disease enters a farm. An animal can look healthy and still carry germs or parasites. Buy from known, healthy farms, ask for the animal's vaccination and treatment history, and avoid animals from markets or areas with disease reports.
Quarantine means keeping new or returning animals in a separate pen, away from your herd or flock, for a period your vet advises, often a few weeks. Care for them last each day, with separate boots and tools, and watch them daily. Ask your vet whether to test, treat or vaccinate before they join the others. Animals that come back unsold from a market or show also go into quarantine.
Dead animals spread disease to your animals, dogs, wild animals and neighbours. Never sell, eat or give away an animal that died of an unknown cause. Handle carcasses with gloves, then dispose of them as your vet or local rules say: often a deep pit, away from water and houses, that dogs and wild animals cannot dig up. If an animal died suddenly, or several are sick, do not open the carcass or move it off the farm: call the vet first, because it may be a notifiable disease or anthrax.
Step by step:
- Buy only from known, healthy farms; ask for the health history.
- Prepare a separate quarantine pen, away from the herd or flock.
- Keep new and returning animals there for the time your vet advises.
- Care for them last each day, with separate boots and tools.
- Choose a disposal place for carcasses with your vet, away from water and houses.
- Sudden or unexplained deaths: do not open or move the carcass; call the vet.
Words to know:
- Quarantine: keeping new or returning animals apart for a time to see whether they carry disease.
- Carcass: the body of a dead animal.
- Notifiable disease: a disease that the law says must be reported to the veterinary authority.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good practices for biosecurity in the pig sector (Animal Production and Health Paper 169)
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Mark a quarantine pen on your farm sketch, as far from your animals as you can, and write how long your vet advises keeping new animals there (ask if you do not know). Then mark where and how you will dispose of dead animals, and write the rule for sudden deaths.
You can now quarantine new animals and dispose of dead animals safely, and know when to call the vet before touching a carcass.

check.q: You buy three goats at the market. What do you do when you get home?
options: Put them straight in with your herd
Keep them in a separate pen for the time your vet advises
Let them graze with the neighbour's goats
check.why: Quarantine shows whether new animals carry disease before they can infect your herd.

check.q: A pig dies suddenly overnight. What is the right first step?
options: Open it to see what happened
Leave the carcass where it is, keep people and animals away, and call the vet
check.why: A sudden death may be a notifiable disease; opening or moving the carcass can spread it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: African Swine Fever and avian influenza: spot, stop, report
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the warning signs of African Swine Fever and avian influenza and report them to the vet at once.
This lesson builds toward: When pigs or poultry show warning signs or die suddenly, you will identify the signs of African Swine Fever or avian influenza and report them to the vet or veterinary authority, at once, without moving, selling or eating the animals.
African Swine Fever (ASF) is a virus disease of pigs that has caused heavy losses in several African countries, including Nigeria. WOAH lists high fever, weakness, loss of appetite, red or purple patches on the skin, vomiting, diarrhoea, abortion in sows and death, with up to 100 percent of pigs dying in severe forms. It spreads through contact with sick pigs, pork and food waste (swill) from infected pigs, and contaminated clothes, boots, vehicles and equipment, and soft ticks where they live. The virus survives a long time in pork and in the environment. It does not infect people. FAO says there is no effective vaccine or treatment, so prevention is the only control; WOAH warns against sub-standard vaccines, so never use an "ASF vaccine" that your national veterinary authority has not approved.
Avian influenza (bird flu) is a virus disease of birds. Severe forms can kill most of a flock in days. Signs listed by USDA APHIS include sudden deaths without warning, birds that are weak and stop eating, a drop in eggs or soft-shelled eggs, swollen and purple comb, wattles and legs, gasping, coughing and twisted necks. It spreads from wild birds, sick birds, live bird markets, droppings, crates, feed, water and equipment. People rarely catch it, mostly through close contact with sick birds, so never handle sick or dead birds with bare hands.
Both diseases are notifiable: suspected cases must be reported to your vet or veterinary authority at once. Only a laboratory test can confirm them, because other diseases look similar. To prevent them: never feed pigs uncooked swill, buy only from healthy farms, keep pigs penned and poultry housed away from wild birds, and use your biosecurity plan every day. If you suspect either disease: keep all animals in, stop all sales and movement of animals, meat, eggs and manure, keep visitors out, and call the vet.
Step by step:
- Know the signs of ASF (pigs) and avian influenza (poultry).
- Check your animals every day.
- Suspect a case: keep all animals in their pens or houses.
- Stop all sales and movements: animals, meat, eggs, manure, equipment.
- Do not open, sell or eat sick or dead animals; no bare hands.
- Call your vet or veterinary office at once and follow their instructions.
Words to know:
- African Swine Fever (ASF): a deadly virus disease of pigs with no effective vaccine or treatment; it does not infect people.
- Avian influenza: bird flu: a virus disease of birds; severe forms kill most of a flock.
- Swill: food waste fed to pigs; uncooked swill with pork can spread ASF.
- Veterinary authority: the government office in charge of animal disease, such as the national or county veterinary services.
Official sources:
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): African swine fever
- FAO: African swine fever (no effective vaccine or treatment; prevention is the control)
- WOAH (June 2025): use only high-quality ASF vaccines that meet the new standard
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): Avian influenza
- USDA APHIS: Avian influenza (signs in birds)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page biosecurity plan. Use your farm sketch with zones, the footbath and visitor rules, quarantine and dead animal disposal, then add the warning signs of ASF or avian influenza, your first-hour actions, and your vet's name and phone number.
You can now recognise the warning signs of African Swine Fever and avian influenza, stop all movement, and report suspected cases to the vet at once.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Zones and entry No sketch, or animals and vehicles mix with no marked zones. Sketch shows clean, buffer and dirty zones, one entry point and where trucks stop. Also shows the route for feed, manure and dead animals so they never cross the clean zone. Footbath and visitor rules No footbath or visitor rules, or rules nobody can follow. Footbath with disinfectant mixed as the label says, handwashing, and a visitor log with last farm visited. Farm-only boots and clothes, and a named person who checks the rules daily. Quarantine and dead animals New animals join the herd at once, or carcasses are sold, eaten or dumped. Separate quarantine pen for the time the vet advises, and a safe disposal place agreed with the vet. Also covers animals returning from market and the rule never to open a suddenly dead animal. ASF or avian influenza response Warning signs missing, or the plan says to sell, treat or wait. Lists the warning signs and the first-hour actions: keep animals in, stop all movement, report at once. Names the veterinary office, phone number and the person who will call, and the no-swill or wild-bird rule. Breeding and new stock New breeding animals are bought with no checks, or the plan allows related matings. New breeding stock comes from known, healthy farms and the plan avoids related matings. Uses AI from unrelated bulls or a male exchange plan, with records of parents. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Several of your pigs have a high fever, purple skin patches and two died overnight. What do you do first?
options: Sell the rest quickly before they die
Buy an ASF vaccine from the market
Keep all pigs in, stop all movement and sales, and call the vet at once
check.why: These are warning signs of ASF, a notifiable disease: stop movement and report it immediately.

check.q: Which practice helps keep African Swine Fever out?
options: Buying pigs from any passing trader
check.why: Uncooked food waste can contain pork with the ASF virus, which survives a long time in meat.
